posts.image_prompt: Towering curved dry-stone granite walls of an ancient African enclosure, neatly stacked stones without mortar, a conical stone tower inside, savanna grass and msasa trees, golden hour light, wide cinematic shot
posts.caption:
🏰 THE STONE CITY THEY SAID AFRICANS COULDN'T BUILD

In southern Africa stand the ruins of Great Zimbabwe — a city built and rebuilt between roughly the 11th and 15th centuries.

Its Great Enclosure has walls about 11 metres high and around 250 metres long. Every stone was stacked by hand. No mortar holds them together.

Archaeologists have found Chinese porcelain and Persian glass there, proof that this inland city was tied into Indian Ocean trade.

Yet when European explorer Karl Mauch saw the ruins in 1871, he refused to believe local people built them and linked them to King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Later colonial authorities pushed the same idea.

The evidence says otherwise. Archaeologists concluded the city was built by the ancestors of the Shona people. In 1980, the newly independent nation named itself after it: Zimbabwe.

Why do you think the truth was resisted for so long?

posts.title: The island that invented writing — and lost it

scenes.narration: So did Rapa Nui invent writing on its own? Tell us what you think, and follow for more.

posts.caption:
🗿 A script no one alive can read.

Rongorongo was carved on wooden tablets on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). Fewer than 30 objects survive, and the script remains undeciphered. A 2024 study dated the wood of one tablet to around 1493–1509 — centuries before European contact.

posts.image_prompt: A glamorous 1940s Hollywood actress in an elegant dress sitting at a drafting table at night, sketching mechanical diagrams, warm lamp light, film-noir atmosphere, no text
posts.caption:
🎬 THE MOVIE STAR WHO PATENTED A SECRET SIGNAL

In the 1940s, Hedy Lamarr was one of Hollywood's most famous faces. Few people knew she was also an inventor.

During World War II she worked with composer George Antheil on a way to stop radio-controlled torpedoes from being jammed: make the signal hop between multiple frequencies, so an enemy couldn't lock onto it.

On August 11, 1942, they received U.S. Patent No. 2,292,387 for a 'Secret Communication System'. The National Inventors Council showed little interest at the time.

Years later, the idea surfaced in military communications — including on U.S. ships during the 1962 blockade of Cuba. Frequency hopping is now seen as an important step in wireless communication.

In 1997 the Electronic Frontier Foundation honoured her work, and in 2014 she was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.

Who's another inventor history forgot to credit?
